frames.narration: A shop app has 8 known bugs: 3 in pricing logic, 3 where components meet, 2 in user journeys. The team will try different mixes of unit, integration and end-to-end tests against them.
First try: 200 unit tests and nothing else. They run in 200 cost units and never fail by themselves. They catch the 3 pricing bugs, because that logic is what they run.
The other 5 bugs ship. A repository replaced by a stub never meets the real columns, and no unit test clicks a button. The suite is green and production is not.
Second try, the other extreme: 60 end-to-end tests. They can see 6 of the 8 bugs, but they cost 9,000 units and 47 of 50 runs fail on their own, through timing and browser noise.

A red build now means little. People re-run until it is green, and that habit is how a real failure gets merged. The two bugs this suite cannot see, a tax threshold and a payment timeout, ship as well.
Third try, the pyramid: 60 unit, 12 integration and 3 end-to-end tests. Unit tests take the 3 logic bugs, integration tests the 3 seams, and the 3 browser tests the 2 journeys.
The cost is 750 units, and 13 of 50 runs are still red from the 15 slower tests, far fewer than the 47 of the browser-heavy suite. Each bug was found at the cheapest layer that can see it.

The ice-cream cone, with 5 unit, 5 integration and 60 browser tests, also catches 8 of 8, but for 9,105 units and 47 red runs of 50. Same coverage of bugs, much higher price. The mix, not the count, is what matters.
